scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Stave dancing originated in the south-west of England during the mid-nineteenth century, arising from friendly society 'club walks' in Somerset, Dorset, and Wiltshire.
Friendly societies were fraternal organizations that provided sickness and death benefits while organising annual social parades, church services, and dinners.
Members and stewards carried decorated ceremonial staves, which evolved into dance props as participants performed country dances and step dances along parish bounds and at village stops.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Stave dancing took place during annual friendly society 'club walks' on Whit-Monday and Midsummer's Day, as well as community weddings.
Staves carried symbolic weight as emblems of civic authority and fraternal unity.
Competitive step dancing displays following annual dinners allowed local dancers to demonstrate agility and pride in their society's regional traditions.
Today it is a revived tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dances are performed in mixed sets of four, six, eight, or more dancers who carry a four- to six-foot stave over the right shoulder while executing English country dance figures.
Basic steps include double-stepping, a traveling polka or 'ranting' step, and the Dorset skip-change step.
While staves are primarily carried on the shoulder, specific figures involve forming elevated arches, twirling staves overhead, or raising staves in a overhead square formation known as a 'rose'.
Watch for Rose figure, Stave arch, Overhead twirl.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Historical costume reflected friendly society rules requiring members to wear 'Sunday best'.
Stewards typically wore black tailcoats, blue sashes, top hats decorated with blue ribbons or knots, and white moleskin trousers.
Staves were wooden poles between four and six feet long, painted or striped like barber poles, topped with brass or wooden emblems and blue ribbons.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Roy Dommett, a scientist and folk dance researcher, recovered historical references and manuscripts (including notes collected by Maud Karpeles) in the 1970s and re-choreographed stave dances.
He introduced these routines to sides such as Bath City Morris and Abercorn Morris, establishing the modern revival.
Regional variations centered on specific villages in Dorset and Somerset.
Stave dancing bridges Victorian friendly society civic ritual and English social country dance.

wardrobe.policy: the narrator wears the dance's traditional apparel, reconstructed meticulously and respectfully from the sources
wardrobe.from_sources: Historical costume reflected friendly society rules requiring members to wear 'Sunday best'. Stewards typically wore black tailcoats, blue sashes, top hats decorated with blue ribbons or knots, and white moleskin trousers. Staves were wooden poles between four and six feet long, painted or striped like barber poles, topped with brass or wooden emblems and blue ribbons. Performance settings included outdoor parish perambulations, village halts, church walks, and marquee tents after annual dinners. Modern teams often reproduce these Victorian steward costumes.
